title: The Smile of Harrow Glen
premise: Folklorist Lior Coldharbour has spent twelve years in Harrow Glen documenting songs the villagers refuse to sing twice, telling themselves the house's noises are settling timber and the village's coldness is ordinary insularity. When every mirror begins reflecting the room one second late, Lior realizes the house has been keeping a ledger of invitations—and that their grandmother, the last Coldharbour, invited something in before she died, something that has been waiting for an heir to acknowledge it. As the frost writes patterns across the windows that mirror the songs' missing verses, Lior uncovers the truth: the entity is not a predator but a neglected guardian spirit bound by duty, starving for belonging. In the final hours before sunrise on the winter solstice, Lior must choose between banishing it as duty demands and giving it what no Coldharbour ever offered—recognition and love—which transforms the haunting into a homecoming.
about_author: Sebastian Ishikawa is a former archivist of regional folk music who spent a decade transcribing songs in remote northern villages before turning to fiction. He writes horror rooted in the belief that the scariest things in old houses are the obligations we inherit along with them.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Rooms
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Twelve years into living at Coldharbour House, Lior records villager Edith Marlowe singing a harvest song she will never repeat, then returns home to sounds in the walls that have always had explanations. The beat is quiet unease: routine as armor.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. While shaving, Lior notices their reflection lags—a raised hand answered a heartbeat too late. Testing every mirror in the house confirms it: all of them, always exactly one second. The emotional beat is denial curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Songs Refused Twice
chapters.summary: Lior's POV in the village archive. Reviewing twelve years of recordings, Lior discovers every informant stopped mid-verse at the same line—the one about 'the guest beneath the frost.' The beat is the first crack in the rationalist facade.

chapters.title: Edith's Warning
chapters.summary: Alternating Lior and Edith POV. Edith visits uninvited, sees the frost patterns on the windows, and goes white: 'It's writing to you now.' She leaves without finishing her tea. The beat is the village's fear made personal.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Searching the attic, Lior finds their grandmother Maren's journal, its final pages written in a hand that isn't hers, recording an invitation: 'Come in from the cold. You may stay.' The beat is horrified inheritance.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Show
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The reflections begin showing the room as it was decades ago—Maren young, singing to someone unseen by the fire. The lag widens to two seconds. The beat is grief entangled with terror.

chapters.title: The Village Closes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Shopkeepers stop meeting Lior's eyes; the pub goes quiet on entry. Old Tam finally says: 'Coldharbours don't leave. That's the arrangement.' The beat is exile within belonging.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Verse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, night. The frost completes a pattern matching the forbidden verse, and for the first time Lior hears the house sing it back—in Maren's voice. The beat is terrible intimacy.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Tam's POV, 1961 flashback. Young Tam watched Maren Coldharbour bargain with the village elders: the thing stays bound to the house, the village stays safe, and no one speaks of it. The beat is complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Hunger in the Walls
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The house grows desperate—doors opening, warmth draining, mirrors showing the reflection mouthing words Lior can't hear. The beat is pity beginning to displace fear.

chapters.title: The Missing Verse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV in the parish records. Lior finds the full song in a 19th-century hymnal: it isn't a ward at all but a lullaby, sung to keep the guest content. The last verse was cut out deliberately. The beat is revelation as indictment.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Maren's POV, 1989 flashback. Dying and alone, Maren invited the entity fully in—not to bind it but because she was lonely, then panicked and tried to reneg, binding it instead. The beat is inherited guilt made flesh.

chapters.title: The Second Night
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The solstice approaches; the mirrors show three seconds of lag and a figure standing behind Lior that isn't there when they turn. The beat is the point of no return.

chapters.title: Running Is an Invitation
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior tries to leave; the road circles back to the house no matter the direction taken. The village watches from lit windows, unmoving. The beat is claustrophobic despair.

chapters.title: Edith's Debt
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith confesses she once sang the full verse as a child and has owed the house silence ever since. She gives Lior the missing lines her mother taught her. The beat is courage passed like contraband.

chapters.title: The Long Dark
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Solstice night begins. The house manifests fully: frost inside the glass, breath on the neck, Maren's voice pleading through the walls. Lior lights every candle and waits for sunrise. The beat is endurance as defiance.

chapters.title: The Guest Beneath the Frost
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, climax part one. At midnight the entity appears—not monstrous but gaunt, patient, wearing the shape of everyone who ever refused it. It asks only the question Maren never answered: 'May I belong?' The beat is terror meeting tenderness.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, climax part two. Sunrise nears; speaking the binding rite would banish it forever. Instead Lior sings the complete lullaby, all verses, alone and unafraid—an act of welcome, not warding. The beat is the choice that defines them.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Dawn comes; the mirrors reflect in perfect time, then show the figure standing beside Lior's reflection, warm-faced, home. The frost on the windows melts into a single word: 'Stay.' The beat is release.

chapters.title: The Village Opens
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The villagers arrive at dawn expecting ruin and find Lior alive, the house warm. Tam weeps; Edith finishes her tea. The arrangement is rewritten aloud, together. The beat is communal reckoning.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, spring. Lior records the villagers singing the full lullaby twice through, willingly, for the first time in a century. The house hums along. The beat is healing without forgetting.

chapters.title: The Smile of Harrow Glen
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Lior's POV. A new family arrives seeking lodging; Lior greets them at the door while something kind moves in the mirrors, one second early now, anticipating joy. The beat is inheritance transformed: belonging freely given.
